claim: Marrow adipose tissue (MAT) is vital for regulating metabolism and maintaining skeletal homeostasis in the bone marrow (BM) niche.
source: Marrow adipose tissue (MAT) has been shown to be vital for regulating metabolism and maintaining skeletal homeostasis in the bone marrow (BM) niche.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that summarizes the established role of MAT based on prior research.

claim: MAT is highly responsive to nutrient fluctuations, hormonal changes, and metabolic disturbances such as obesity and diabetes mellitus.
source: As a reflection of BM remodeling, MAT is highly responsive to nutrient fluctuations, hormonal changes, and metabolic disturbances such as obesity and diabetes mellitus.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about MAT's responsiveness to various physiological conditions.

claim: Expansion of MAT has been strongly associated with bone loss in mice and humans.
source: Expansion of MAT has also been strongly associated with bone loss in mice and humans.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on prior research establishing the correlation between MAT expansion and bone loss.

claim: Adipsin is the most upregulated adipokine during MAT expansion in mice and humans in a PPARγ acetylation-dependent manner.
source: We show that Adipsin is the most upregulated adipokine during MAT expansion in mice and humans in a PPARγ acetylation-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from mouse models and human samples.

claim: Genetic ablation of Adipsin in mice specifically inhibited MAT expansion but not peripheral adipose depots.
source: Genetic ablation of Adipsin in mice specifically inhibited MAT expansion but not peripheral adipose depots, and improved bone mass during calorie restriction, thiazolidinedione treatment, and aging.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data from Adipsin KO mice in multiple experimental models.

claim: Genetic ablation of Adipsin improved bone mass during calorie restriction, thiazolidinedione treatment, and aging.
source: Genetic ablation of Adipsin in mice specifically inhibited MAT expansion but not peripheral adipose depots, and improved bone mass during calorie restriction, thiazolidinedione treatment, and aging.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by bone density measurements in Adipsin KO mice across multiple models.

claim: Adipsin's effects on MAT and bone are mediated through its downstream effector, complement component C3.
source: These effects were mediated through its downstream effector, complement component C3, to prime common progenitor cells toward adipogenesis rather than osteoblastogenesis through inhibiting Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding supported by experiments with C3 KO mice and in vitro studies.

claim: Adipsin primes common progenitor cells toward adipogenesis rather than osteoblastogenesis through inhibiting Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: These effects were mediated through its downstream effector, complement component C3, to prime common progenitor cells toward adipogenesis rather than osteoblastogenesis through inhibiting Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding supported by in vitro differentiation studies and molecular analyses of Wnt signaling components.

claim: Calorie restriction induces shrinkage of most adipose tissue depots but paradoxically expands MAT in the femur.
source: CR is a broadly adapted intervention for metabolic improvements. It induces the shrinkage of most adipose tissue depots, but, paradoxically, expands MAT as in the femur (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by osmium tetroxide staining shown in Figure 1A and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Cfd (encoding Adipsin) is among the top induced genes by CR in the BM and is the most abundant among all secretory genes.
source: Interestingly, Cfd (encoding Adipsin) is among the top induced genes by CR in the BM and is the most abundant among all secretory genes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CR induced an approximately ninefold induction of Cfd in the BM compared to ad libitum-fed mice.
source: qPCR analysis validated an approximately ninefold induction of Cfd in the BM by CR compared to ad libitum-fed mice, accompanied by increased adipocyte genes (Pparg2, Fabp4, Plin1) and decreased osteoblast markers (Osteocalcin, Col1a1) (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CR increased adipocyte genes (Pparg2, Fabp4, Plin1) and decreased osteoblast markers (Osteocalcin, Col1a1) in the BM.
source: qPCR analysis validated an approximately ninefold induction of Cfd in the BM by CR compared to ad libitum-fed mice, accompanied by increased adipocyte genes (Pparg2, Fabp4, Plin1) and decreased osteoblast markers (Osteocalcin, Col1a1) (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Protein levels of Adipsin are notably increased in bone after CR.
source: In the bone, protein levels of Adipsin are also notably increased after CR (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Plasma Adipsin was not significantly increased in CR mice.
source: However, the upregulation of BM Adipsin, even though it is more pronounced and at a higher abundance than Adiponectin, is unlikely to contribute significantly to the circulating levels, as plasma Adipsin was not significantly increased in CR mice (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and quantification data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Adipsin is uniquely regulated in the BM, highlighting its potential role in regulating the BM microenvironment.
source: This data suggests that, unlike other adipokines, Adipsin is uniquely regulated in the BM, highlighting its potential role in regulating the BM microenvironment.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential regulation of Adipsin in BM versus peripheral tissues.

claim: Rosiglitazone treatment induced profound MAT expansion in DIO mice.
source: This condition could induce profound MAT expansion, as indicated by a significant increase of osmium tetroxide staining of lipid droplets (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by osmium tetroxide staining shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Cfd expression in the BM was upregulated >12-fold by Rosi treatment, more than other adipocyte markers.
source: In this model, Cfd expression in the BM was upregulated >12-fold, more than other adipocyte markers (e.g., Pparg2 and Fabp4) and Adiponectin (Adipoq) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Perilipin 1 (Plin1) was robustly induced by Rosi treatment in the BM, indicating abundant MAT expansion.
source: Increased expression of Perilipin 1 (Plin1) was also robustly induced by Rosi treatment in the BM, indicating abundant MAT expansion (Styner et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data and is consistent with prior literature cited.

claim: Neither trabecular nor cortical bone mineral density (BMD) was decreased by short-term (3-week) Rosi treatment.
source: In contrast, neither the trabecular nor the cortical bone mineral density (BMD) was decreased by short-term Rosi treatment (Figure 1K, L).
evidence: This is supported by μCT scan data shown in Figures 1K and 1L.

claim: BM adipogenesis precedes significant bone loss by TZD treatment.
source: This data suggests that BM adipogenesis precedes the significant bone loss by TZD and that BMAd-derived factors, such as Adipsin, may participate in regulating downstream changes in the bone.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the temporal dissociation between MAT expansion and bone loss observed in the short-term Rosi treatment.

claim: Adipsin KO mice displayed significantly lower bone marrow adiposity (BMA) upon CR.
source: Upon CR, Adipsin KO mice displayed significantly lower bone marrow adiposity (BMA) detected by osmium tetroxide staining for lipid droplets (Figure 2A, B)
evidence: This is supported by osmium tetroxide staining and quantification shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Adipsin KO mice showed decreased expression of adipogenesis markers in the BM upon CR.
source: The inhibited MAT was underlined by decreased expression of adipogenesis makers in the BM, including Pparg, Adipoq, Fabp4, Fasn, Gdp1, and Perilipin (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Adipsin KO mice preserved more fat mass during CR despite similar response to CR on overall body weight, insulin sensitivity, and glucose tolerance.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to their reduced BMA, Adipsin KO mice preserved more fat mass, despite the similar response to CR on overall body weight, insulin sensitivity, and glucose tolerance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by body composition and metabolic testing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Adipsin KO mice showed higher BMD in the cortical and trabecular regions upon CR.
source: In line with their lower BMA, Adipsin KO mice showed higher BMD in the cortical and trabecular regions (Figure 2D, E)
evidence: This is supported by μCT scan data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: No significant changes of MAT or bone structure were observed in adult Adipsin KO mice on ad libitum chow diet feeding.
source: It should be noted that no significant changes of MAT or bone structure were observed in adult Adipsin KO mice on ad libitum chow diet feeding (Figure 2A–F)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 2A–F comparing chow-fed WT and Adipsin KO mice.

claim: Adipsin KO mice showed fewer lipid droplets accumulated in the BM after Rosi treatment.
source: H&E staining revealed fewer lipid droplets accumulated in the Adipsin KO mouse BM (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Ablation of Adipsin improved skeletal health as shown by higher BMD in both the cortical and trabecular femoral regions upon Rosi treatment.
source: Furthermore, ablation of Adipsin improved skeletal health as shown by higher BMD in both the cortical and trabecular femoral regions without affecting BV (Figure 2I–L)
evidence: This is supported by μCT scan data shown in Figures 2I–L.

claim: Adipsin deficiency alters the balance between MAT expansion and bone homeostasis in distinct bone loss models, leading to an overall bone protection effect.
source: Thus, Adipsin deficiency appears to consistently alter the balance between MAT expansion and bone homeostasis in distinct bone loss models, leading to an overall bone protection effect.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the consistent phenotypes observed across multiple models (CR, Rosi, aging).

claim: Adipsin is also called Complement Factor D.
source: Adipsin, also called Complement Factor D (Rosen et al., 1989; White et al., 1992), is an established activator of Complement Component 3 (C3), the central player of the complement system (Xu et al., 2001; Sahu and Lambris, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Adipsin is an established activator of Complement Component 3 (C3), the central player of the complement system.
source: Adipsin, also called Complement Factor D (Rosen et al., 1989; White et al., 1992), is an established activator of Complement Component 3 (C3), the central player of the complement system (Xu et al., 2001; Sahu and Lambris, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: C3 deficiency protects mice from ovariectomy-induced bone loss.
source: C3 deficiency has been shown to protect mice from ovariectomy-induced bone loss (MacKay et al., 2018).
evidence: This is prior research cited to support the investigation of C3 in the current study.

claim: C3 KO mice displayed a pronounced inhibition of MAT expansion upon CR.
source: Despite no discernible differences in body weight or composition and worse insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance but similar fasting insulin levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E), C3 KO mice displayed a pronounced inhibition of MAT expansion (Figure 3A, B)
evidence: This is supported by osmium tetroxide staining and quantification shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: C3 KO mice showed increases in cortical BMD and cortical thickness upon CR.
source: In contrast to MAT, the effects on bone were overall mild (Figure 3C–F), with increases observed only in cortical BMD (Figure 3C) and cortical thickness (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is supported by μCT scan data shown in Figures 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: Complement activity is critical to BM adipogenesis in response to CR.
source: These data indicate that complement activity is critical to BM adipogenesis in response to CR.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the inhibited MAT expansion in C3 KO mice upon CR.

claim: C3 knockout restrained the development of MAT in baseline HFD-fed, obese mice.
source: In baseline HFD-fed, obese mice C3 knockout restrained the development of MAT as shown by osmium tetroxide staining (Figure 3G, H) without affecting BMD (Figure 3J, K).
evidence: This is supported by osmium tetroxide staining and μCT scan data shown in Figures 3G, H, J, K.

claim: C3 deficiency prevented Rosi-induced MAT expansion by an approximately sixfold reduction.
source: Strikingly, C3 deficiency prevented Rosi-induced MAT expansion by an approximately sixfold reduction (Figure 3G, H), further supported by observed differences in H&E staining (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by osmium tetroxide staining, quantification, and H&E staining shown in Figures 3G, H, I.

claim: C3 KO mice displayed strong protection of cortical BMD and BV (BV/TV) in both the cortical and trabecular regions upon Rosi treatment.
source: Additionally, C3 KO mice displayed strong protection of cortical BMD (Figure 3J) and BV (BV/TV) in both the cortical and trabecular regions (Figure 3L, M)
evidence: This is supported by μCT scan data shown in Figures 3J, L, M.

claim: The inhibition of MAT expansion and bone loss in Adipsin KO mice is amplified in C3 KO mice.
source: Together, the inhibition of MAT expansion and bone loss in Adipsin KO mice is amplified in C3 KO mice, suggesting that Adipsin plays a role in regulating marrow homeostasis through complement activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparing the phenotypes of Adipsin KO and C3 KO mice.

claim: Adipsin in the circulation gradually decreased during aging.
source: Aging is associated with MAT expansion and decline in bone integrity (Krings et al., 2012). Interestingly, Adipsin in the circulation was gradually decreased during aging (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cfd was markedly upregulated in the BM at 78 weeks of age compared to middle-aged (26-week-old) mice.
source: Indeed, Cfd was markedly upregulated in the BM at 78 weeks of age compared to middle-aged (26-week-old) mice (Figure 4B), in striking contrast to the decrease in the peripheral fat (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: BM Adipsin is distinct from peripheral Adipsin and is uniquely correlated with BMA and bone health during aging.
source: These data emphasize that BM Adipsin is distinct from peripheral Adipsin and is uniquely correlated with BMA and bone health during aging.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential regulation of Adipsin in BM versus peripheral tissues during aging.

claim: Aging Adipsin KO mice displayed an approximately 50% decrease in BMA.
source: Similar to the CR model, the osmium tetroxide staining in the femur revealed an approximately 50% decrease in BMA in Adipsin KO mice (Figure 4D, E)
evidence: This is supported by osmium tetroxide staining and quantification shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: Aging Adipsin KO mice displayed significantly higher BMD in the femoral trabecular region.
source: Furthermore, Adipsin KO mice displayed a significantly higher BMD in the femoral trabecular region (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by μCT scan data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The bone protective effects in aging Adipsin KO mice were independent of metabolic changes.
source: These bone protective effects in aging Adipsin KO mice were independent of metabolic changes as their body weight, composition, insulin sensitivity, and glucose tolerance remained comparable to those of WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by metabolic testing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The adipogenic capacity of Adipsin KO BMSCs was diminished even with Rosi activation of PPARγ.
source: Interestingly, even with Rosi activation of PPARγ, the adipogenic capacity of Adipsin KO BMSCs was diminished, shown by decreased Oil Red O staining for lipid droplets and mRNA expression of adipocyte markers (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining and qPCR data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Adipsin KO BMSCs were more readily differentiated into osteoblasts.
source: On the other hand, these cells were more readily differentiated into osteoblasts as determined by increased Alizarin Red staining for mineralization and increased expression of osteoblast markers, including Runx2, Atf4, Osx, Alpl, Ptfhr, Col1a1, and Osteocalcin (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is supported by Alizarin Red staining and qPCR data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: The adipogenic capacity for ASCs from Adipsin KO mice was not hindered.
source: However, the adipogenic capacity for the ASCs from Adipsin KO mice was not hindered indicated by comparable Oil Red O staining and adipogenic gene expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The difference in differentiation capability between BMSCs and ASCs highlights the specific effect of Adipsin on the BM.
source: The difference in differentiation capability between BMSCs and ASCs highlights the specific effect of Adipsin on the BM.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the contrasting differentiation capacities of BMSCs and ASCs from Adipsin KO mice.

claim: C3 KO BMSCs had impaired adipogenesis.
source: Similar to Adipsin KO cells, C3 KO BMSCs had impaired adipogenesis, as shown by lower Oil Red O staining and modest downregulation of markers related to adipogenesis (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining and qPCR data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: The ablation of C3 enhanced osteoblast differentiation capacity.
source: Conversely, the ablation of C3 enhanced osteoblast differentiation capacity, indicated by increased Alizarin Red staining and upregulation of mRNA expression of osteoblastogenesis markers (Figure 5G, H).
evidence: This is supported by Alizarin Red staining and qPCR data shown in Figures 5G and 5H.

claim: Adipsin deficiency directly modulates BMSC fate by hindering their differentiation into adipocytes and favoring osteoblastogenesis through complement activity.
source: Together, these results suggest that Adipsin deficiency directly modulates BMSC fate by hindering their differentiation into adipocytes and favoring osteoblastogenesis through complement activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the in vitro differentiation studies of BMSCs from Adipsin KO and C3 KO mice.

claim: Adipsin KO BMSCs displayed higher expression of genes associated with osteoblastogenesis and repressed adipocyte markers after short-term dexamethasone treatment.
source: Interestingly, at 48 hr post-treatment, Adipsin KO cells displayed a higher expression of genes associated with osteoblastogenesis, including Runx2, Atf4, and Opn, whereas adipocyte markers Adipoq, Fabp4, Fasn, and Cd36 were significantly repressed (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Adipsin KO BMSCs may be primed toward osteoblastogenic differentiation.
source: These data suggest that Adipsin KO BMSCs may be primed toward osteoblastogenic differentiation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the gene expression patterns in Adipsin KO BMSCs after dexamethasone treatment.

claim: The presence of Adipsin in the BM microenvironment primes BMSC fate toward adipogenesis in vivo.
source: As nascent wild-type BMSCs barely express adipogenic genes such as Adipsin, these results further imply that the presence of Adipsin in the BM microenvironment primes BMSC fate toward adipogenesis in vivo.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that Adipsin KO BMSCs are primed toward osteoblastogenesis.

claim: Adipsin treatment repressed the induction of osteoblast markers during osteoblastogenic differentiation of Adipsin KO BMSCs.
source: Adipsin treatment repressed the induction of osteoblast markers during osteoblastogenic differentiation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Exogenous Adipsin had a mild effect on promoting adipocyte differentiation.
source: On the other hand, exogenous Adipsin had a mild effect on promoting adipocyte differentiation, as shown by increased lipid accumulation and upregulation of PPARγ2, the master regulator of adipogenesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Inhibiting C3 complement activity by SB290157 prevented lipid accumulation and repressed adipogenic gene expression during adipogenesis in BMSCs.
source: Conversely, inhibiting the downstream C3 complement activity by SB290157, a C3aR inhibitor, prevented lipid accumulation and repressed adipogenic gene expression during adipogenesis (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, E)
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: SB290157 promoted the upregulation of osteoblast transcription factor Osx during osteoblastogenesis in BMSCs.
source: while promoting the upregulation of osteoblast transcription factor Osx during osteoblastogenesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) in BMSCs.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Treating BMSCs with SB290157 blunted the effects of exogenous Adipsin on their differentiation into adipocytes and osteoblasts.
source: Moreover, treating BMSCs with SB290157 blunted the effects of exogenous Adipsin on their differentiation into adipocytes and osteoblasts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: Complement activity suppression is optimal for osteoblast differentiation and inhibitory of adipogenesis.
source: Together, these data suggest that complement activity suppression is optimal for osteoblast differentiation and inhibitory of adipogenesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the effects of SB290157 on BMSC differentiation.

claim: Adipsin functions in the BM microenvironment to prime BMSCs toward adipocyte differentiation and inhibit osteoblastogenesis.
source: These data support our conclusion that Adipsin functions in the BM microenvironment to prime BMSCs toward adipocyte differentiation and inhibit osteoblastogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the in vitro studies with recombinant Adipsin and SB290157.

claim: Undifferentiated Adipsin KO BMSCs showed notable upregulation in genes associated with the canonical (Wwtr1, Lrp5) and non-canonical Wnt pathways (Wnt5a).
source: We found a notable upregulation in genes associated with the canonical (Wwtr1, Lrp5) and non-canonical Wnt pathways (Wnt5a) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The canonical Wnt pathway is well established to inhibit adipogenesis and promote bone formation.
source: This pathway is well established to inhibit adipogenesis (Park et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2010) and promote bone formation (Gong et al., 2001; Mani et al., 2007; Glass and Karsenty, 2007)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Upregulation of non-canonical-associated proteins induces Runx2 expression.
source: while upregulation of non-canonical-associated proteins induces Runx2 expression (Takada et al., 2007; Tu et al., 2007), the main osteoblastogenic transcriptional factor.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Adipsin likely inhibits Wnt signaling in order to determine the differentiation fate of BMSCs.
source: Thus, Adipsin likely inhibits Wnt signaling in order to determine the differentiation fate of BMSCs.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the upregulation of Wnt pathway genes in Adipsin KO BMSCs.

claim: Adipsin treatment inhibited both the canonical (Lrp5) and non-canonical (Wnt5a) Wnt signaling genes in Adipsin KO BMSCs.
source: Consistently, Adipsin treatment inhibited both the canonical (Lrp5) and non-canonical (Wnt5a) Wnt signaling genes, whereas SB290157 treatment abolished this inhibition in Adipsin KO BMSCs (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Adipsin treatment blunted Wnt3a-induced phosphorylation of GSK3β and prevented the subsequent accumulation of β-catenin in C3H10T1/2 mesenchymal stem cells.
source: In support of this hypothesis, Adipsin treatment blunted Wnt3a-induced phosphorylation of GSK3β and prevented the subsequent accumulation of β-catenin in C3H10T1/2 mesenchymal stem cells (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Adipsin KO mice displayed increased GSK3β phosphorylation in the bone after Rosi treatment.
source: Furthermore, the activation of canonical Wnt signaling was recapitulated in Adipsin KO mice, which displayed increased GSK3β phosphorylation in the bone (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Immunohistochemical staining revealed an increase in β-catenin in the BM of Adipsin KO mice after Rosi treatment.
source: Though β-catenin signal was too low to be detected by western blotting, immunohistochemical staining revealed an increase in β-catenin in the BM of Adipsin KO mice (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway genes Wnt3a, Fzd9, and Ctnnb1 were upregulated in the BM of Adipsin KO mice after Rosi treatment.
source: Additionally, Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway genes Wnt3a, Fzd9, and Ctnnb1 (Rudloff and Kemler, 2012), but not the β-catenin-repressive Tcf3 and Tcf7l2, were upregulated in the BM of Adipsin KO mice after Rosi treatment (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: C3 KO mice showed increases in GSK3β phosphorylation, β-catenin, and expression of Wnt pathway genes in the bone after Rosi treatment.
source: We also observed increases in GSK3β phosphorylation, β-catenin, and expression of Wnt pathway genes in the bone of C3 KO mice after Rosi treatment (Figure 6J–L)
evidence: This is supported by western blot, immunohistochemical staining, and qPCR data shown in Figures 6J–L.

claim: Adipsin inhibits Wnt signaling through its complement activity to prime BMSCs toward adipocyte differentiation.
source: Together, these data imply that Adipsin inhibits Wnt signaling through its complement activity to prime BMSCs toward adipocyte differentiation.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the Wnt signaling studies in Adipsin KO and C3 KO mice and cells.

claim: Adipsin is induced during adipogenesis by PPARγ, the master regulator of adipocyte biology.
source: Adipsin is induced during adipogenesis by PPARγ, the master regulator of adipocyte biology (Tontonoz et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Adipocyte-specific ablation of PPARγ leads to significantly increased trabecular bone density with an associated absence of BMA accompanied by a lipoatrophy phenotype.
source: Adipocyte-specific ablation of PPARγ leads to significantly increased trabecular bone density with an associated absence of BMA accompanied by a lipoatrophy phenotype (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is prior research cited to support the investigation of PPARγ regulation of Adipsin.

claim: Adipocyte-specific PPARγ KO mice displayed a complete absence of circulating Adipsin.
source: Notably, these knockouts displayed a complete absence of circulating Adipsin (Figure 7A), suggesting that PPARγ is essential for Adipsin production.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: PPARγ is essential for Adipsin production.
source: Notably, these knockouts displayed a complete absence of circulating Adipsin (Figure 7A), suggesting that PPARγ is essential for Adipsin production.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the absence of circulating Adipsin in adipocyte-specific PPARγ KO mice.

claim: Adipsin levels in the EWAT and in circulation were markedly decreased in the PPARγ deacetylation-mimetic 2KR mice.
source: As predicted, Adipsin levels in the EWAT and in circulation were markedly decreased in the PPARγ deacetylation-mimetic 2KR mice, while other adipokines and adipocyte markers, such as Adiponectin and aP2, were not as significantly altered (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The decrease of circulating Adipsin in 2KR mice was supported by prevalent repression of Cfd in three major adipose depots – EWAT, SWAT, and BAT.
source: This decrease of circulating Adipsin was supported by prevalent repression of Cfd in three major adipose depots – EWAT, SWAT, and brown adipose tissue (BAT) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C) as well as in the BM of 2KR mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: The 2KR model largely recapitulates the bone protection and inhibited MAT expansion effect observed in adipocyte conditional PPARγ KO mice but without the previously observed lipoatrophy.
source: Of note, the 2KR model largely recapitulates the bone protection and inhibited MAT expansion effect observed in adipocyte conditional PPARγ KO mice but without the previously observed lipoatrophy (Kraakman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research cited.

claim: The repression of Adipsin in PPARγ mutant mouse models is consistent with the inhibited BMA and improved skeletal health observed in Adipsin KO and C3 KO models.
source: The repression of Adipsin in these two PPARγ mutant mouse models is consistent with the inhibited BMA and improved skeletal health observed in Adipsin KO and C3 KO models.
evidence: This is an interpretation linking the PPARγ mutant phenotypes to the Adipsin and C3 KO phenotypes.

claim: The Adipsin promoter was activated >300-fold by WT PPARγ in a luciferase reporter assay.
source: In HEK293T cells, Adipsin promoter was activated >300-fold by WT PPARγ in a luciferase reporter assay, while the 2KR mutant showed a much weaker transcriptional activity, especially in response to activation by Rosi treatment (Figure 7C)
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The 2KR mutant showed much weaker transcriptional activity on the Adipsin promoter, especially in response to activation by Rosi treatment.
source: In HEK293T cells, Adipsin promoter was activated >300-fold by WT PPARγ in a luciferase reporter assay, while the 2KR mutant showed a much weaker transcriptional activity, especially in response to activation by Rosi treatment (Figure 7C)
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: WT PPARγ directly bound to the Adipsin promoter while the 2KR mutation impaired this binding at multiple regions.
source: We further showed that WT PPARγ directly bound to the Adipsin promoter while the 2KR mutation impaired this binding at multiple regions, particularly in the regions of −448 to −355 bp, −252 to −110 bp, and −114 to +33 bp identified by ChIP in comparably differentiated adipocytes (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The −281 to +35 bp region of the Adipsin promoter accounted for major promoter activation by PPARγ.
source: Further manipulation of the promoter by truncated deletions revealed that the −281 to +35 bp region accounted for major promoter activation by PPARγ, with a sequence at −165 to −50 bp necessary for maximal promoter activity (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data with promoter deletions shown in Figures 7E–G.

claim: A sequence at −165 to −50 bp of the Adipsin promoter is necessary for maximal promoter activity.
source: Further manipulation of the promoter by truncated deletions revealed that the −281 to +35 bp region accounted for major promoter activation by PPARγ, with a sequence at −165 to −50 bp necessary for maximal promoter activity (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data with promoter deletions shown in Figures 7E–G.

claim: PPARγ deacetylation on Lys268 and Lys293 impairs the recruitment of PPARγ to the Adipsin promoter, underlying the repressed expression.
source: Thus, PPARγ deacetylation on Lys268 and Lys293, though localized to the ligand-binding domain (LBD), impairs the recruitment of PPARγ to the Adipsin promoter, underlying the repressed expression.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the ChIP and luciferase reporter assay data.

claim: Fasting is a potent signal that can induce an increase in MAT in humans.
source: In human, fasting is a potent signal that can induce an increase in MAT.
evidence: This is established knowledge that sets up the analysis of human BMAd samples.

claim: Vertebral MAT increased 8.1 ± 2.6% (p=0.01) at day 10 of fasting in human volunteers.
source: By spectroscopy, vertebral MAT increased 8.1 ± 2.6% (p=0.01) at day 10 and bone resorption increased by 77% (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is data from a previous clinical trial cited in the manuscript.

claim: Bone resorption increased by 77% (p<0.0001) at day 10 of fasting in human volunteers.
source: By spectroscopy, vertebral MAT increased 8.1 ± 2.6% (p=0.01) at day 10 and bone resorption increased by 77% (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is data from a previous clinical trial cited in the manuscript.

claim: Complement activation was the second most upregulated pathway from pre- to post-10 day fast in human BMAds.

A similar finding was recapitulated in human BMAds after a 10-day fast.
